chief_complaint: mouth itching, lip swelling, and throat scratching after eating raw apples
hpi_details: 41M reports that for the past year, he experiences immediate itching and mild swelling of his lips, tongue, and throat whenever he eats raw apples, peaches, or cherries. Can eat cooked apple pie without any symptoms.
ideas: thinks he has a dangerous fruit allergy
concerns: worried about throat closing when eating fruit
expectations: wants to know why cooked fruit is fine

clinical_knowledge.topic: Oral Allergy Syndrome (Pollen-Food Allergy Syndrome) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Oral allergy syndrome (pollen-food allergy syndrome) results from IgE cross-reactivity between inhaled pollen proteins and structurally similar, heat-labile proteins in certain raw fruits and vegetables.
Birch pollen sensitization commonly cross-reacts with apple, peach, cherry, and other Rosaceae fruits, producing itching and mild swelling confined to the mouth, lips, and throat.
Symptoms are typically triggered only by the raw form of the food because cooking or peeling denatures the heat-labile allergen, so the same fruit eaten cooked is usually tolerated.
Systemic reactions are uncommon but can occur, so patients should be counseled on red-flag symptoms and, in select cases, may be prescribed an epinephrine auto-injector.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: mouth itching, lip swelling, and throat scratching after eating raw apples

Key HPI features: 41M reports that for the past year, he experiences immediate itching and mild swelling of his lips, tongue, and throat whenever he eats raw apples, peaches, or cherries. Can eat cooked apple pie without any symptoms.
Objective/Exam findings: Mild lip or oral mucosal swelling may be seen during an active reaction; exam is typically normal between episodes, with no stridor or hives.
Relevant background/PMH: Allergic rhinitis (severe birch pollen allergy)
common_misconceptions: Assuming any raw-fruit reaction must be a dangerous, primary IgE food allergy requiring strict avoidance of the food in all forms.
Ordering food-specific IgE or skin testing with commercial fruit extracts, which can give false-negative results because the relevant proteins degrade in extract preparation.
Reassuring the patient that all fruit exposure is equally safe without asking whether the cooked form is tolerated.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to true (primary) fruit allergy — reacts even to cooked fruit — without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Symptoms spreading beyond the mouth (hives, throat tightness, breathing trouble) — suggests a true systemic allergy instead.
management_principles: Explain the cross-reactivity mechanism and heat-lability of the causative fruit proteins.
Advise avoiding the raw form of trigger fruits, or peeling/cooking them, since this usually eliminates symptoms.
Reassure that this is generally distinct from a primary, potentially life-threatening food allergy, while reviewing red-flag symptoms that would warrant reassessment.
Consider prescribing an epinephrine auto-injector for patients with risk factors for progression to a systemic reaction.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 41M reports that for the past year, he experiences immediate itching and mild swelling of his lips, tongue, and throat whenever he eats raw apples, peaches, or cherries. Can eat cooked apple pie without any symptoms.
reference_soap.objective: Mild lip or oral mucosal swelling may be seen during an active reaction; exam is normal between episodes, with no stridor, hives, or other systemic findings.
reference_soap.assessment: Oral allergy syndrome (pollen-food allergy syndrome) due to birch pollen and fruit-protein cross-reactivity.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Explain the cross-reactivity mechanism and heat-lability of the causative proteins. 2. Advise avoiding raw forms of trigger fruits, or peeling/cooking them. 3. Discuss red-flag symptoms that would indicate a systemic reaction rather than oral allergy syndrome. 4. Consider an epinephrine auto-injector given his history of oropharyngeal symptoms. 5. Refer to Allergy for confirmatory testing if the diagnosis remains unclear.

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features and diagnostic criteria of oral allergy syndrome (pollen-food allergy syndrome).
Formulate a prioritized differential diagnosis for mouth itching, lip swelling, and throat scratching after eating raw apples
Distinguish oral allergy syndrome from a primary, potentially systemic fruit allergy
Implement evidence-based counseling and management for pollen-food allergy syndrome due to birch-fruit cross-reactivity.

teaching.one_liner: Cross-reactivity between birch pollen and heat-labile proteins in raw fruits, causing itching confined to the mouth and throat that resolves once the fruit is cooked.
differentials: True (primary) fruit allergy — reacts even to cooked fruit
red_flags: Symptoms spreading beyond the mouth (hives, throat tightness, breathing trouble) — suggests a true systemic allergy instead

must_ask.say: Do you react to raw apples but tolerate cooked apple, like in a pie?
Does the reaction stay in your mouth and throat, or spread anywhere else?
Do you have hay fever or a pollen allergy, especially to birch trees?
Do other raw fruits like peaches or cherries cause the same thing?
Has this ever caused hives, swelling beyond your mouth, or trouble breathing?

history.answer: Whenever I eat raw apples, my lips and mouth start itching and swelling up, so I came in to find out what is going on.
This started about one year ago, and it happens every single time I take a bite of fresh fruit.
It starts almost instantly, usually within two or three minutes of chewing and swallowing raw fruit.
The itching is mainly on my lips, tongue, roof of the mouth, and the back of my throat.
It feels like an intense prickling itch and scratchiness, and my lips feel mildly puffy for a little while.
The sensation usually peaks quickly and then fades away on its own within thirty to forty-five minutes.
Raw apples always trigger it, but if I eat baked apple pie or applesauce, I do not get any symptoms at all.
Yes, I noticed the exact same tingling and lip swelling with fresh peaches and fresh cherries.
No, I have never passed out, felt dizzy, or had a full-body reaction from eating fruit.
My throat feels scratchy and irritated inside, but I have never had trouble breathing, gasping, or wheezing.
No, I have never broken out in hives, welts, or widespread rashes after eating fruit.
No, I have not had any stomach cramps, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea after eating them.
No, I have never felt faint, lightheaded, or clammy during these episodes.
No, I have had no fever, chills, or night sweats.
No, my weight has been completely steady and I have good energy.
This has happened several times over the past year whenever I try raw stone fruits or apples, but I have not had formal allergy testing yet.
I took an over-the-counter allergy pill once and it seemed to calm the tingling faster, but usually I just drink cold water and wait it out.
I have bad seasonal hay fever every spring, especially when birch trees are blooming, with bad sneezing and a runny nose.
It makes me anxious whenever I eat salads or fruit bowls at work, so I have been completely avoiding fresh fruit.
I am wondering if I developed a dangerous fruit allergy that could suddenly turn life-threatening.
My biggest worry is that one day my throat might completely swell shut if I accidentally eat a piece of apple.
I really want to understand why cooked apple pie causes zero trouble while raw apples make my mouth swell.
I have seasonal allergic rhinitis, but I have never had asthma or any other chronic medical conditions.
I have never had any surgeries and I have never been hospitalized.
I take cetirizine ten milligrams as needed during the spring when my seasonal allergies act up.
I do not have any known allergies to prescription medications or over-the-counter drugs.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used e-cigarettes in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of beer on weekends with friends, nothing heavy.
I work in an office as an accountant, and I live in an apartment with my wife and son.
My mother has seasonal pollen allergies and hay fever, but no one in my family has severe food allergies.

No cervical or submandibular lymphadenopathy palpated; trachea is midline and non-tender.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally across all lung fields without wheezes, crackles, or stridor.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs heard.
